author: John Stuart Mill
title: Utilitarianism
openingText: Among the circumstances that make up the present state of human knowledge, few are more unlike what we might have expected, or tell us more about the backward state in which speculation on the most important subjects still lingers, than how little progress has been made in settling the controversy over the criterion of right and wrong. From the dawn of philosophy, the question of the _summum bonum_, or in other words the foundation of morality, has been counted the main problem of speculative thought. It has occupied the most gifted minds and divided them into sects and schools, which have waged vigorous war on one another. After more than two thousand years the same discussions continue, and philosophers are still ranged under the same contending banners. Neither thinkers nor mankind at large seem any nearer to unanimity on the subject than when the young Socrates listened to the old Protagoras and argued the theory of utilitarianism against the popular morality of the so-called sophist (if Plato's dialogue is based on a real conversation).
about:
What makes an action right? Mill defends the principle of utility: actions are right insofar as they tend to promote happiness, and wrong insofar as they tend to produce its opposite. Happiness here means pleasure and the absence of pain. The happiness of everyone concerned counts, not merely the agent's own.

Across five chapters, Mill explains the principle, asks what can motivate us to follow it, and considers what sort of proof can support it. He distinguishes the quality of pleasures from their quantity and examines how justice and rights relate to general utility.

Published as a book in 1863, the work defends a theory while answering objections to it. Watch the distinctions between ends and means, intention and motive, and the consequences of a particular act and general rules. The footnotes belong to the argument, including Mill's clarification of intention and motive.

angleCards.title: Quality and quantity
angleCards.text: Mill argues that pleasures differ in more than quantity. His test of quality uses the judgment of people acquainted with both kinds. He also considers why people may nevertheless choose the lower pleasure.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine whether experienced people's preferences can establish differences in the quality of pleasures.

angleCards.title: Desired and desirable
angleCards.text: In Chapter Four, Mill moves from what people actually desire to what is desirable. Follow the argument and ask whether the transition is justified.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to test Mill's argument for happiness as the only ultimate end.

angleCards.title: Why follow morality?
angleCards.text: Chapter Three examines conscience, education and social feeling. It asks how moral feelings develop and what gives them power over our actions.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand how Mill connects moral obligation with feelings and social life.

angleCards.title: Justice and rights
angleCards.text: The final chapter examines rights, punishment, pay and taxation. Mill tries to explain why justice makes stronger demands than ordinary considerations of usefulness.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to judge whether Mill can justify the special protection of rights through general utility.

cast.name: John Stuart Mill
cast.description: Mill explains and defends utilitarianism through arguments, examples and replies to critics. He asks readers to distinguish the theory's standard for action from the motives that actually move people to act.

cast.name: The Greatest Happiness Principle
cast.description: Actions are judged by their tendency to promote happiness or its opposite. The agent's own happiness does not count more than anyone else's. Mill also includes other sentient beings within morality's ultimate aim.

cast.name: Jeremy Bentham
cast.description: Mill links Bentham to the name Greatest Happiness Principle and to the requirement that everyone count equally. His notes also emphasize Bentham's distinction between intention and motive and his deductions from human nature.

cast.name: The competent judges
cast.description: These are people acquainted with both pleasures being compared and able to appreciate them. Mill relies on their considered preference, or the majority's where they disagree, rather than on a single person's momentary choice.

cast.name: Socrates dissatisfied
cast.description: Mill says it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. The comparison distinguishes happiness from mere contentment and explains why higher capacities can remain valuable despite greater vulnerability.

whyItMatters.title: Weighing personal and shared interests
whyItMatters.body: The book examines a morality in which one's own happiness does not automatically take priority over other people's. It asks what this requires of individuals and society.

whyItMatters.title: Rules and particular cases
whyItMatters.body: Mill does not think every action must begin with a fresh calculation of the world's happiness. He considers how experience supports general rules and what happens when rules conflict.

whyItMatters.title: A foundation for rights
whyItMatters.body: The chapter on justice connects rights with security and social protection. Readers can examine the strength of that connection and its limits when competing considerations arise.
